Riidiger J. Seitz 
Bettina Blank

Stiff-person syndrome with anti-glutamic 
acid decarboxylase autoantibodies: 
complete remission of symptoms 
after intrathecal baclofen administration 
Received: 2 December 1994 
Received in revised form: 9 February 1995 
Accepted: 16 February 1995 
R. J. Seitz • B. Blank • R. Benecke (~) 
Department of Neurology, 
Heinrich-Heine-University, 
D-40001 Dtisseldorf, Germany 
J. C. W. Kiwit 
Department of Neurosurgery, 
Heinrich-Heine-University, 
Dtisseldorf, Germany 
Abstract A female patient, aged 61 
years, who developed a severe im- 
mobilizing stiff-person syndrome in 
conjunction with insulin-dependent 
diabetes mellitus, is described. In ad- 
dition to the typical clinical symp- 
toms, diagnosis was proven by the 
presence of autoantibodies against 
glutamic acid decarboxylase in 
serum and cerebrospinal fluid. 
Symptomatic treatment with continu- 
ous intrathecal application of ba- 
clofen administered by a subcuta- 
neous pump resulted in rapid clinical 
improvement so that the patient be- 
came ambulatory. Intermittent with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen 
therapy led to complete remanifesta- 
tion of stiff-person syndrome within 
18 h; after re-introduction of in- 
trathecal therapy stiffness disap- 
peared completely within 48 h. The 
clinical course has been stable now 
for over 24 months and stiffness has 
completely disappeared. The effect 
of baclofen in this patient is dis- 
cussed in the light of the suggested 
pathophysiological mechanisms in 
stiff-person syndromes. 
Key words Stiff-person syndrome • 
Intrathecal baclofen • Anti-glutamic 
acid decarboxylase autoantibodies 
Introduction 
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare, usually slowly pro- 
gressive, disorder of the central nervous system which, as 
originally described by Moersch and Woltmann [24], is 
characterized by stiffness mainly of axial and proximal 
muscles, startle reactions with sudden spasms, and ab- 
sence of other neurological signs. Electromyography 
(EMG) typically shows persistent motor unit activity in 
axial muscles indistinguishable from normal voluntary ac- 
tivity [5, 18, 22]. Pathophysiologically, hyperactivity of 
spinal motoneurons seems to result from disinhibition due 
to selective functional and/or degenerative changes of 
spinal interneurons [15, 31, 32]. Grimaldi and coworkers 
[12] suggested that SPS is a heterogeneous disorder and 
can be subdivided into three main subgroups: (1) patients 
who have associated autoimmune diseases and positive 
tests for islet-cell autoantibodies and anti-glutamic acid 
autoantibodies (organ-specific autoantibodies); (2) pa- 
tients who have associated neoplasms and no organ-spe- 
cific autoantibodies but non-organ specific autoantibod- 
ies; and (3) patients without neoplasm and only non-organ 
specific autoantibodies. Both GABA A agonists such as di- 
azepam, and GABA B agonists, such as baclofen, have 
been shown to reduce stiffness in cases of SPS [22]. 
Pathoanatomical support for the hypothesis of a defect 
in the GABA system has been derived from the demon- 
stration of autoantibodies against glutamic acid decar- 
boxylase (GAD) in the serum of patients with SPS, since 
this enzyme catalyses the conversion of glutamate to 
GABA [2, 4, 21, 29]. These autoantibodies have been 
found in serum as well as in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of

about 60% of patients with SPS. Interestingly, autoanti- 
bodies to GAD cross-react with [3-cells of the pancreas, 
explaining the 58% prevalence of insulin-dependent (type 
1) diabetes mellitus in SPS [12]. 
Oral treatment of SPS with GABA agonists at a dosage 
high enough to suppress the muscular hyperactivity is of- 
ten hampered by systemic side-effects such as drowsiness

619 
and vertigo. We report a patient with severe SPS whose 
stiffness was abolished when treated with intrathecal ad- 
ministration of the GABA B agonist baclofen. 
Case report 
One and a half years earlier, this 61-year-old woman had devel- 
oped chronically progressive painful stiffness of the musculature 
of her body, sparing arms and facial musculature. This stiffness 
initially included only the legs, but spread subsequently to the ab- 
domen, back and neck. Eventually, the patient could not walk or 
even sit. In addition, she complained of startle reactions with sud- 
denly increasing muscle stiffness caused by unexpected acoustic, 
visual or tactile stimuli. 
At the age of 40 years, the patient had developed type 1 dia- 
betes mellitus with greatly fluctuating blood sugar levels. Over the 
years, a diabetic retinopathy and a chronic compensated renal fail- 
ure had supervened. Autoimmune diseases were not known in the 
family. A biopsy of the gastrocnemius muscle performed else- 
where and an ascending lumbar myelography had revealed no ab- 
normality. Finally, the patient was admitted to our hospital. 
The bedridden patient was in a moderate general and nutri- 
tional condition. Her cranial nerves were normal. She was not able 
to bend her neck forwards. She could not move her legs at the hip, 
knee or ankle joints because of extreme muscle stiffness. The ab- 
dominal wall was hard as if with peritonitis. Hyperlordosis - often 
a feature of SPS - was not observed. There were no pareses or at- 
rophies. The tendon reflexes were normal in the upper and lower 
extremities, but induced severely painful muscle spasms of axial 
and leg muscles when elicited in the lower extremities. Plantar re- 
flexes were flexor. On sensory examination we found a distally 
pronounced mild diabetic polyneuropathy of the lower extremities 
involving all modalities except position sense. Coordination of her 
arms was normal, as were the findings of neuropsychological and 
psychopathological examinations. 
EMG showed continuous muscle activity similar to voluntary 
action. Electroneurography demonstrated a mild polyneuropathy 
of both sensory and motor nerves of the lower extremities, com- 
patible with the existing type 1 diabetes mellitus. Magnetic evoked 
motor potentials to the first interosseus and the tibialis anterior 
muscles were normal in amplitude and latency. Cranial MRI dis- 
closed some small white matter lesions of vascular origin on both 
sides. Except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 
50/90 mm in the first two hours, blood sugar levels up to 800 mg/dl 
and reduced creatinine clearance (37 ml/min) with a corresponding 
elevation of creatinine to 1.5 mg/dl, routine laboratory findings were 
normal, including electrophoresis, C-reactive protein, rheumatoid 
factor, antinuclear antibodies, thyroid autoantibodies, thyroid hor- 
mones and treponemal agglutination test. Except for slightly posi- 
tive oligoclonal bands the cerebrospinal fluid was normal (cell 
count 3/mm 3, protein level 0.36 g/l, Delpeche ratio 0.49). GAD an- 
tibodies, as detmwnined immunocytochemically according to Soli- 
mena and coworkers [29], were strongly positive in CSF and 
serum. 
Having made the diagnosis of SPS by clinical and electrophys- 
iological criteria [5, 18, 22, 24] and demonstration of anti-GAD 
autoantihodies [12], we injected 2 mg diazepam intravenously, 
whereupon muscle tone and backache promptly diminished. The

patient could move her legs and bend her neck again (Fig. 1 ). None 
of the following intravenously administered drugs reduced the 
muscle tone or the painful spasms: insulin, isosorbide dinitrate, 
nifedipine, omeprazole, heparin, pethidine, buprenorphine, meta- 
mizole, diclofenac. Clonazepam and baclofen were then given 
orally at dosages of 1.5 mg and 20 mg daily, respectively, leading 
to improved mobility and relief of painful spasms. Higher doses 
were not tolerated and resulted in drowsiness. However, the patient 
was still unable to walk. Thereafter, bolus injections of up to 100 
btg baclofen were given intrathecally on consecutive days. Follow- 
ing injection of 75 gg, muscle tone decreased and backache im- 
proved further. After an even more successful injection of 1000 btg 
the patient received a subcutaneous port system in the epigastric 
region for continuous intrathecal application of baclofen. Baclofen 
was infused to titrate the required dosage further. With this treat- 
ment the patient started to walk, using crutches. After 2 weeks the 
port was removed and a pump subcutaneously implanted (Infusaid, 
Norwood, USA). With this pump a daily dosage of 260 btg ba- 
clofen was administered. A slightly higher dosage of 300 btg daily

Fig. 2 Polyelectromyographic recordings before (A), during with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) and 48 h after recon-

the marked increase of muscle activity 18 h after onset of with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) 
resulted in drowsiness and nausea. Oral administration of clon- 
azepam and baclofen was discontinued. After 4 weeks of con- 
comitant physical therapy the patient's condition improved pro- 
gressively and she was finally able to walk with crutches (Fig. 1). 
Furthermore, effective immunosuppressive therapy with azathioprine 
(lymphocytes < 1000/gl) was initiated about 10 weeks after the 
start of the baclofen treatment. After a 12-month course of contin- 
uous treatment the patient had improved further: the gait pattern 
had normalized and only one crutch was needed (Fig. 1). At that 
time GAD autoantibodies were still detected in serum but were 
only weakly present in CSF. After 24 months her condition had 
stabilized further: gait was now normal, without crutches. At that 
time immunosuppression had to be discontinued because of severe 
lymphopenia. 
To prove that the intrathecal treatment with baclofen was still 
effective the patient was hospitalized and the baclofen therapy in- 
terrupted. Within 18 h the signs of SPS reappered to such a degree 
that the patient was no longer able to walk. Surface EMG record- 
ings from trunk and leg muscles again showed the typical sponta- 
neous muscle activity. After restoring the intrathecal baclofen ther- 
apy with the above-mentioned dosage of 260 gg the patient recov- 
ered completely within 48 h (Fig. 2). 
Discussion 
Treatment of SPS has been mainly symptomatic, consist- 
ing of benzodiazepines (diazepam and clonazepam), ba- 
clofen and valproate, given orally or intravenously. As al- 
ready known from spastic and dystonic disorders [10, 25, 
27], intrathecal application of baclofen is more efficient 
and has fewer side effects than oral administration. This is 
because the lipophilic substance baclofen can easily cross 
the blood-brain barrier and was administered directly onto 
the lumbar spinal cord yielding a high local concentration 
and a lower concentration at the level of the brain stem 
and the brain [8]. Physiologically, baclofen induces a de- 
crease of the mono- and polysynaptic reflexes, as demon- 
strated by a dramatic reduction of the H reflex and of the 
F waves [10]. In our patient, both diazepam and baclofen 
resulted in improvement of her severe disability. The most 
remarkable observation, however, was a permanent com- 
plete remission of muscle stiffness with preservation of 
full muscle force so far for more than 2 years. Drug with- 
drawal immediately resulted in a relapse that could, how- 
ever, completely be reversed by restoring the intrathecal 
baclofen supply. 
For theoretical reasons complete relief of symptoms 
can only be expected when the cause is treated or when 
symptomatic treatment interacts with the dominant patho- 
physiological process of a disease. As we have learned

621 
from Parkinson's disease, partial degeneration of a neu- 
ronal system can take place in the presence of the thera- 
peutic effect of levodopa treatment. Benefit, however, is 
greater when the amount of cell degeneration is relatively 
small. In SPS it can be suggested that the anti-GAD au- 
toantibody leads to a functional and/or degenerative dis- 
turbance of GABAergic neurons. As far as the symptoma- 
tology of SPS is concerned, mainly spinal inhibitory in- 
terneurons may be affected, followed by disinhibition of 
spinal motoneurons. It is intriguing and not apparently 
clear, however, why in patients with anti-GAD autoanti- 
bodies either separate type 1 diabetes mellitus or SPS or a 
combination of both diseases occurs, and why GABAer- 
gic neurons in other parts of the central nervous system, 
especially the brain, are not affected in most cases of SPS, 
In some patients diagnosed as having SPS, however, un- 
usual symptoms such as oculomotor disturbances, posi- 
tive Babinski sign, tremor, cerebellar deficits, epilepsy or 
dementia may hint at an affliction of supraspinal 
GABAergic neurons [3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 17, 19, 20, 23, 24, 
29]. Furthermore, in a recent paper [26] the presence of 
serum antibodies directed against GAD was reported in a 
patient with epilepsy and palatal myoclonus not associ- 
ated with brain lesions. One explanation for the hetero- 
geneity of symptoms in patients with anti-GAD autoanti- 
bodies could be derived from the presence of different 
GAD isoforms in various neuronal tissues. The mam- 
malian brain contains two forms of GAD to synthesize the 
inhibitory transmitter GABA, GAD65 and GAD67. 
GAD67 is present throughout the neuron, whereas 
GAD65 is concentrated in synaptic terminals, suggesting 
that it may act as a synaptic GAD reservoir [16]. 
Taking for granted that in the autoimmune form of SPS 
with anti-GAD autoantibodies there is a selective degen- 
eration of GABAergic spinal inhibitory interneurons, suc- 
cessful treatment of SPS with baclofen could be envis- 
aged as a substitution therapy similar to dopamine ago- 
nist therapy in Parkinson's disease. Baclofen activates 
GABA B receptors which are present both on the presy- 
naptic terminals of primary afferents and on the postsy- 
naptic membranes of interneurons but not on motoneu- 
rons in the spinal cord [7, 28]. The depression of a volt- 
age-dependent Ca ~+ inward current produced by binding 
of baclofen to GABA B receptors on afferent fibres is 
thought to inhibit the release of excitatory transmitters 
(presynaptic inhibition) [8]. The increased K + conduc- 
tance and its accompanying hyperpolarization produced 
by activation of GABAB receptors on spinal interneurons 
significantly reduce the ability of excitatory synaptic cur- 
rents to produce action potentials. They decrease the abil- 
ity of such interneurons to participate in spinal reflex re- 
sponses. On the basis of complete relief of stiffness by ba- 
clofen in our patient, the obviously separate stimulation of 
GABA B receptors is sufficient to restore the function of 
GABAergic intemeurons. Similarly, separate stimulation 
of GABA a receptors by benzodiazepines leading to an in- 
crease of the GABA-induced C1 current may have the 
same effect [8]. Meinck and coworkers [22] also de- 
scribed a beneficial effect of intrathecal baclofen therapy 
in two patients with anti-GAD autoantibodies. In contrast 
to our patient, however, there was no complete relief of

stiffness. Their patients had suffered from stiffness for 
more than 5 years before treatment, whereas our patient 
had had a relatively short history of 1.5 years before in- 
trathecal therapy was started. It may turn out that early 
treatment with intrathecally applied baclofen is more ben- 
eficial than late treatment when the autoimmunological 
destructive process may be more advanced. In patients 
with GAD autoantibodies the therapeutic regimen may 
thus benefit from additional plasmapheresis, administra- 
tion of intravenous immunoglobulins or immunosuppres- 
sion, which have all been shown to be effective in single 
patients [1, 13, 30]. One could hypothezise that early in 
the disease GABAergic neurons, still active, are highly re- 
sponsive to their natural endogenous and to externally in- 
troduced homologue ligands. 
In summary, evidence is presented that early intrathe- 
cal treatment with baclofen is extremely successful in SPS 
with anti-GAD autoantibodies and is superior to oral 
treatment with baclofen and benzodiazepines because of 
the absence of systemic side-effects in lifelong therapy. 
Whether patients with paraneoplastic SPS and idiopathic 
SPS without anti-GAD autoantibodies also react to the 
same extent remains to be established and will be the sub- 
ject of future investigations. 
Acknowledgement We thank W. H. Oertel, University of Mu- 
nich, in whose laboratories the measurements of the GAD autoan- 
tibodies in serum and CSF of our patient were carried out.

Fig. 2 Polyelectromyographic recordings before (A), during with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) and 48 h after recon- 
tinuation (C). Calibrations are in mV and ms, respectively. Note 
the marked increase of muscle activity 18 h after onset of with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) 
resulted in drowsiness and nausea. Oral administration of clon- 
azepam and baclofen was discontinued. After 4 weeks of con- 
comitant physical therapy the patient's condition improved pro- 
gressively and she was finally able to walk with crutches (Fig. 1). 
Furthermore, effective immunosuppressive therapy with azathioprine 
(lymphocytes < 1000/gl) was initiated about 10 weeks after the 
start of the baclofen treatment. After a 12-month course of contin- 
uous treatment the patient had improved further: the gait pattern 
had normalized and only one crutch was needed (Fig. 1). At that 
time GAD autoantibodies were still detected in serum but were 
only weakly present in CSF. After 24 months her condition had 
stabilized further: gait was now normal, without crutches. At that 
time immunosuppression had to be discontinued because of severe 
lymphopenia. 
To prove that the intrathecal treatment with baclofen was still 
effective the patient was hospitalized and the baclofen therapy in- 
terrupted. Within 18 h the signs of SPS reappered to such a degree 
that the patient was no longer able to walk. Surface EMG record- 
ings from trunk and leg muscles again showed the typical sponta- 
neous muscle activity. After restoring the intrathecal baclofen ther- 
apy with the above-mentioned dosage of 260 gg the patient recov- 
ered completely within 48 h (Fig. 2).
